title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Compartments and Meninges
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the coverings of the brain and spinal cord, the spaces between them, the dural folds that divide the skull into compartments, the circulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the barriers that separate blood from brain and CSF, and the interpretation of a CSF sample. Board questions give a mechanism of injury, a CT shape, a pupil, or a CSF panel and ask you to name the space, the vessel, the compressed structure, or the organism class. Each answer follows from which layer is attached where, which opening lies next to which structure, and what inflammation does to the barriers.

Epidural and subdural hematomas and the herniation they cause are the main mechanisms of death after head injury.

terms.def: The three membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord: dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater.
A space that exists only when fluid or blood separates two layers that are normally in contact.
A venous channel between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the cranial dura that drains blood and CSF from the brain.
A cerebral vein that crosses the subdural space from the cortex to a dural venous sinus.
Displacement of brain tissue from one intracranial compartment into another through a rigid dural or bony opening.
Because the adult skull is rigid, the volumes of brain, blood, and CSF are fixed in sum, so an increase in one must be offset by a decrease in another.
A wide region of the subarachnoid space where the arachnoid bridges over a deep surface contour.
A tuft of arachnoid that projects into a dural venous sinus and returns CSF to venous blood.
The diffusion barrier formed by tight junctions between nonfenestrated brain capillary endothelial cells.
A small region beside the third or fourth ventricle with fenestrated capillaries and no blood-brain barrier.
Yellow discoloration of CSF from hemoglobin breakdown products, indicating blood that entered the CSF hours or more before the tap.
Raised CSF protein with a normal or near-normal white cell count.

sections.title: Meninges, meningeal spaces, and intracranial hemorrhage

blocks.text: The space a bleed occupies follows from which layer is attached to which, and from which vessel breaks. The dura mater is the tough outer layer. In the skull it has an outer periosteal layer, which is the inner periosteum of the bones, and an inner meningeal layer; the two are fused except where they separate to enclose the dural venous sinuses, and the meningeal layer folds inward to form the falx and tentorium (C02). The cranial dura is pain sensitive (mainly trigeminal above the tentorium, upper cervical and vagal below).

The arachnoid mater is a thin avascular membrane held against the dura by CSF pressure; its outer arachnoid barrier cells are joined by tight junctions, and fine trabeculae cross from it to the pia. The pia mater is a delicate vascular layer that adheres to the brain and spinal cord and follows every sulcus.

The epidural space lies between bone and dura. In the skull it is only a potential space, because the periosteal dura is the lining of the bone, so it opens only when blood strips the dura away. The spinal dura has no periosteal layer, so the vertebral canal has a real epidural space containing fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus. The subdural space is also a potential space: dura and arachnoid are joined by a weak layer of dural border cells, and this layer splits when blood collects. The subarachnoid space is a real space between arachnoid and pia that holds CSF and the large arteries and veins of the brain surface.

Trauma overall; ruptured berry aneurysm when spontaneous

blocks.caption: The vessel sets the tempo; dural attachments set the shape.

blocks.text: In epidural hematoma, the middle meningeal artery (a branch of the maxillary artery that enters through the foramen spinosum) is torn where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet. Subdural blood is venous and low pressure. Brain atrophy in older adults and in chronic alcohol use stretches the bridging veins, so minor trauma tears them, and shaking injures infants the same way. Spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage puts arterial blood directly into CSF, usually from a saccular aneurysm at a branch point of the circle of Willis, most often near the anterior communicating artery. Blood irritates the meninges, red cells appear in the CSF, and xanthochromia develops over hours as hemoglobin is broken down to bilirubin. Blood around the arteries later triggers vasospasm, most often about 3 to 10 days after the bleed.

blocks.title: Epidural hematoma

Some patients are lucid while the clot enlarges

blocks.caption: Arterial source explains both the lucid interval and the speed of decline.

blocks.predict: A crescent-shaped collection over one hemisphere crosses the coronal suture but ends sharply at the midline. Which space is it in?
blocks.explain: Subdural. Blood under the meningeal dura is not held by sutures, which bind only the periosteal dura to bone, but it cannot cross the falx, which is a fold of the meningeal dura itself.

sections.title: Dural folds, intracranial pressure, and herniation

blocks.text: The meningeal dura folds inward to form rigid partitions. The falx cerebri is a sickle-shaped sheet in the longitudinal fissure between the hemispheres, running from the crista galli to the tentorium; its attached upper border carries the superior sagittal sinus, and its free lower border, which arches above the corpus callosum, carries the inferior sagittal sinus. The tentorium cerebelli roofs the posterior cranial fossa, separating the occipital lobes from the cerebellum and dividing the cranial cavity into supratentorial and infratentorial compartments. Its free anterior edge bounds the tentorial notch, the only opening between the two compartments, through which the midbrain passes.

Because the adult skull is rigid, brain, blood, and CSF share a fixed volume (the Monro-Kellie doctrine). An expanding mass is first offset by pushing CSF into the spinal subarachnoid space and blood out of the venous sinuses, so intracranial pressure (about 5 to 15 mm Hg in a supine adult) hardly changes. Once these reserves are used, small added volumes raise pressure steeply. Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure, so the rise causes ischemia. Ischemia of the medulla triggers a sympathetic surge that raises blood pressure, the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart, and breathing becomes irregular (the Cushing triad).

blocks.title: Rising intracranial pressure
steps: Mass expands after CSF and venous reserves are used
blocks.caption: Edema from ischemia adds volume and raises pressure further, which is why decline can accelerate.

blocks.text: Pressure is not shared evenly. Brain moves from the higher-pressure compartment through a rigid opening, and the structures at that opening determine the signs (table below). In uncal herniation the medial temporal lobe slides over the tentorial edge and presses the oculomotor nerve against the edge or the posterior cerebral artery. Its parasympathetic pupillary fibers run on the outside of the nerve, so the ipsilateral pupil dilates and stops reacting before ptosis and a down-and-out eye appear; ischemic third nerve palsy in diabetes damages the core of the nerve and usually spares the pupil. Compression of the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle gives contralateral hemiparesis because the corticospinal tract has not yet crossed, and midbrain compression of the reticular activating system lowers consciousness. Downward stretch can tear paramedian branches of the basilar artery, causing Duret hemorrhages in the midbrain and pons. Removing CSF by lumbar puncture when a mass is present can create the pressure gradient that drives tonsillar herniation.

blocks.caption: Each opening has a fixed neighbor, so the compressed structure predicts the deficit.

blocks.title: Which side is the lesion?
blocks.text: A man with a right temporal epidural hematoma becomes drowsy. His right pupil is dilated and fixed. The uncus herniates on the side of the mass, so the right CN III is compressed, and the pupil localizes correctly. Weakness should be on the left, from the right cerebral peduncle. If instead the right arm and leg are weak, the shift has pushed the left cerebral peduncle against the opposite tentorial edge (Kernohan notch), damaging left corticospinal fibers above their crossing. Weakness then appears ipsilateral to the mass and falsely localizes. The pupil is the more reliable sign of side.

sections.title: Cisterns, CSF circulation, and the lumbar cistern

blocks.text: The pia follows every contour of the brain, but the arachnoid bridges over deep grooves, leaving wide pools of CSF called cisterns. They hold arteries and cranial nerves, so blood from a ruptured aneurysm collects in them, and they receive CSF as it leaves the fourth ventricle.

blocks.title: Major subarachnoid cisterns
rows: Between the cerebellum and the dorsal medulla
Receives CSF from the median aperture of the fourth ventricle
Oculomotor nerves, basilar bifurcation, posterior circle of Willis
Optic chiasm, anterior circle of Willis
Quadrigeminal (cistern of the great cerebral vein)
Behind the midbrain, above the cerebellum
Conus medullaris (about L1 to L2) to about S2
Cauda equina and filum terminale; site of lumbar puncture
blocks.caption: Cisterns at the base of the brain are where subarachnoid blood is seen on CT.

blocks.text: Choroid plexus in the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles secretes most CSF, about 500 mL per day. Only about 150 mL is present at once, so the volume turns over three to four times daily. The choroid epithelium moves Na+, Cl-, and HCO3- into the ventricles, using a Na+/K+-ATPase on its apical (ventricular) surface and carbonic anhydrase, and water follows through aquaporin-1. Secretion is nearly independent of CSF pressure, so a block anywhere downstream raises pressure upstream.

blocks.title: CSF circulation
steps: Choroid plexus secretes CSF into the lateral ventricles
Interventricular foramina (of Monro) to the third ventricle
Cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle
Median and lateral apertures into the cisterns
Subarachnoid space around brain and spinal cord
Arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus
blocks.caption: Flow is one way, from secretion in the ventricles to absorption into venous blood.

blocks.text: Arachnoid granulations are tufts of arachnoid that push through the dura into the dural venous sinuses, mainly the superior sagittal sinus. Absorption is bulk flow driven by CSF pressure exceeding venous sinus pressure, and the granulations behave as one-way valves, so blood does not enter CSF when venous pressure rises. Some CSF also drains along nerve sheaths to lymphatics. Obstruction inside the ventricular system, as in aqueductal stenosis, causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus; scarring of the granulations after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage causes communicating hydrocephalus.

The vertebral column grows longer than the spinal cord during development, so the adult conus medullaris ends at about L1 to L2 (about L3 at birth). The dural sac and subarachnoid space continue to about S2, forming the lumbar cistern, which contains CSF, the filum terminale, and the floating roots of the cauda equina. A needle at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5 enters the cistern below the cord, and the roots usually slide aside. The line joining the tops of the iliac crests crosses about the L4 spinous process or the L4 to L5 interspace. A midline needle passes skin, subcutaneous tissue, the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, the ligamentum flavum, the epidural space, the dura, and the arachnoid before CSF flows.

blocks.predict: A tumor compresses the cerebral aqueduct. Which ventricles enlarge, and would a lumbar puncture relieve the pressure?
blocks.explain: The lateral and third ventricles enlarge because they are upstream of the block, while the fourth ventricle stays normal. This is noncommunicating hydrocephalus, so the lumbar cistern does not connect with the dilated ventricles, and lowering spinal pressure risks a downward pressure gradient and herniation.

sections.title: Blood-brain barrier, blood-CSF barrier, and circumventricular organs

blocks.text: In most tissues small solutes pass between capillary endothelial cells. Brain capillaries close this route. The blood-brain barrier has three parts: continuous, nonfenestrated endothelial cells sealed by tight junctions (claudin-5 and occludin) with very little vesicular transport; a basement membrane shared with pericytes; and astrocyte foot processes covering nearly the whole capillary surface. The endothelial tight junctions are the actual diffusion barrier. Astrocytes and pericytes induce and maintain these endothelial properties rather than block diffusion themselves.

With the paracellular route closed, a substance must cross the endothelial cell, so lipid solubility, small size, and lack of charge predict entry. Polar nutrients need carriers, and efflux pumps such as P-glycoprotein return many lipid-soluble drugs to blood. Unconjugated bilirubin that is not bound to albumin is lipid soluble and can enter the neonatal brain, staining the basal ganglia (kernicterus).

blocks.title: How substances cross the blood-brain barrier
rows: Glucose by GLUT1; large neutral amino acids and L-dopa by LAT1
Saturable; dopamine has no carrier, so only its precursor enters
H+, HCO3-, proteins, most ions and polar drugs
Central chemoreceptors sense arterial PCO2 rather than acute changes in blood pH
Keeps many drugs and toxins out of the brain
blocks.caption: CO2 diffuses in and is hydrated to H+ near the chemoreceptors, while plasma H+ enters only slowly.

blocks.text: Tumors, abscesses, infection, and infarction open the barrier, so plasma proteins and water leak into brain interstitium (vasogenic edema) and intravenous contrast enhances the lesion. This differs from cytotoxic edema, in which energy failure stops the Na+/K+-ATPase and cells swell behind an intact barrier.

In the choroid plexus the capillaries are fenestrated and leaky, so the barrier moves to the choroid epithelium, modified ependymal cells joined by tight junctions. This blood-CSF barrier, with the arachnoid barrier cells at the outer surface, separates blood from CSF.

Circumventricular organs lie beside the third and fourth ventricles and have fenestrated capillaries and no barrier, because their job requires contact with blood: they sense its composition or secrete hormones into it. Tanycyte-like ependymal cells joined by tight junctions seal them off from the rest of the brain and the CSF.

sections.title: Interpreting CSF in meningitis and Guillain-Barré syndrome

blocks.text: Each CSF value reflects a process. Opening pressure, measured with the patient lying on the side, is normally about 6 to 20 cm H2O. Normal CSF holds up to about 5 white cells per µL, all mononuclear, and no red cells. Protein is about 15 to 45 mg/dL, under 1% of the plasma level, because the barriers exclude large molecules. Glucose is about 50 to 80 mg/dL, roughly 60% of a simultaneous blood glucose, because it enters only by carrier-mediated GLUT1 transport and is continuously taken up by brain cells; a CSF to blood ratio below about 0.4 is clearly low.

Meningitis changes these values in three ways. Inflammation opens the barriers, so protein leaks in, and edema with impaired absorption raises pressure. The cell type reflects the immune response: pyogenic bacteria recruit neutrophils, while viral, fungal, and tuberculous infections are dominated by lymphocytes. Glucose falls when transport across the inflamed barrier is impaired and when leukocytes, bacteria, and inflamed brain consume it by glycolysis, which also raises CSF lactate. Viral meningitis recruits lymphocytes without major glucose consumption, so glucose stays normal.

blocks.title: CSF patterns
rows: About 20 to 500 (lymphocytes); may be few in AIDS
blocks.caption: Values are typical ranges; individual cases overlap, so the pattern is read as a whole.

blocks.text: Patterns overlap. Very early viral meningitis can show neutrophils, partially treated bacterial meningitis can look lymphocytic, and some viruses (mumps, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus) can lower glucose modestly. Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV infection may show few cells because the host cannot mount inflammation, yet pressure is often very high, thought to reflect capsular polysaccharide blocking the arachnoid granulations. Tuberculous meningitis forms a thick, protein-rich basal exudate that can entrap cranial nerves and block CSF flow. Gram stain, culture, cryptococcal antigen, acid-fast stain, and PCR identify the organism.

Guillain-Barré syndrome is an immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, most often demyelinating. The proximal nerve roots run through the subarachnoid space, and their inflamed blood-nerve barrier leaks protein into CSF, but the inflammation is in the nerve, not the meninges, so few cells enter. The result is albuminocytologic dissociation. Protein may still be normal in the first week, and a count above about 50 cells per µL suggests another cause, such as HIV infection, Lyme disease, or lymphoma.

blocks.title: Reading a lymphocytic panel with low glucose
blocks.text: Over three weeks a man develops headache, fever, and a left CN VI palsy. CSF: opening pressure 28 cm H2O, 220 white cells per µL (85% lymphocytes), protein 240 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL with blood glucose 110 mg/dL. Step 1: the ratio is 30/110, about 0.27, so glucose is consumed or excluded, which rules against viral meningitis. Step 2: lymphocytes rather than neutrophils, plus a subacute course, point away from pyogenic bacteria. Step 3: very high protein and a cranial nerve palsy fit a basal exudate, favoring tuberculous meningitis. Cryptococcal antigen and acid-fast testing separate the two remaining options.

blocks.predict: Why does CSF glucose stay normal in viral meningitis but fall in tuberculous meningitis, when both are lymphocytic?
blocks.explain: Glucose falls when the inflamed barrier limits GLUT1 transport and when organisms, leukocytes, and inflamed tissue consume it. Tuberculous meningitis has an intense granulomatous basal exudate that does both; viral meningitis causes milder inflammation with little glucose use.
blocks.check: The paragraph on the three ways meningitis changes CSF.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology set the rules. The periosteal dura bound to bone at sutures shapes an epidural clot, the meningeal dura folds into the falx and tentorium that channel herniation, and differential growth of the vertebral column leaves a lumbar cistern below the conus where a needle can enter safely. Physiology explains pressure: CSF is secreted at a nearly constant rate and absorbed by pressure-driven bulk flow, so any block or added mass inside a rigid skull raises pressure, lowers perfusion, and produces the Cushing triad. Biochemistry and cell biology explain the barriers, with tight junctions, GLUT1, LAT1, and P-glycoprotein deciding what reaches neurons.

Microbiology, immunology, and pathology meet in the CSF panel: the type of organism determines whether neutrophils or lymphocytes are recruited, and the intensity of inflammation determines how far glucose falls and protein rises. CSF values overlap between causes and change with timing and prior antibiotics, and a lumbar puncture in the presence of a mass lesion can itself cause herniation, so the panel is read with the clinical course and imaging.

summary: The epidural space is potential in the skull and real in the spinal canal; the subdural space is a split in the dural border cell layer; the subarachnoid space is real and holds CSF and the major surface vessels.

Epidural hematoma is arterial (middle meningeal artery at the pterion), lens shaped, and stops at sutures; subdural hematoma is venous (bridging veins), crescentic, and crosses sutures but not the falx.
Spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage is usually a ruptured berry aneurysm, often near the anterior communicating artery, with blood and later xanthochromia in the CSF and vasospasm days later.
In a rigid skull, pressure rises steeply once CSF and venous reserves are used; perfusion pressure equals MAP minus ICP, and medullary ischemia produces the Cushing triad.

Subfalcine herniation compresses the anterior cerebral artery; uncal herniation compresses CN III (pupil first), the posterior cerebral artery, and the cerebral peduncle; tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla.
CSF flows from choroid plexus through the ventricles and apertures to the subarachnoid space and returns through arachnoid granulations to the superior sagittal sinus.
The adult cord ends at about L1 to L2 and the dural sac at about S2, so lumbar puncture at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5 enters the lumbar cistern below the cord.

The blood-brain barrier is endothelial tight junctions; the blood-CSF barrier is choroid epithelial tight junctions; circumventricular organs such as the area postrema and posterior pituitary lack a barrier.
Bacterial meningitis gives neutrophils, high protein, and low glucose; viral gives lymphocytes with normal glucose; fungal and tuberculous give lymphocytes with low glucose and high protein.
Guillain-Barré syndrome raises CSF protein without raising cells (albuminocytologic dissociation) because the inflammation is in nerve roots, not the meninges.

verify: Normal CSF values differ between sources: opening pressure upper limit 20 or 25 cm H2O, glucose 40 to 70 or 50 to 80 mg/dL, and a normal CSF to blood glucose ratio of about 0.6 to 0.67; confirm the values NABNE expects.
Cell counts and protein ranges for bacterial, viral, fungal, and tuberculous meningitis are typical ranges with wide overlap; confirm whether NABNE tests specific cutoffs.
CSF production (about 500 mL per day, quoted from about 450 to 600) and volume (about 150 mL) vary slightly between texts.
The window for vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage is quoted as about 3 to 10 days in some sources and 4 to 14 days in others.
The level of the intercristal line is given as the L4 spinous process or the L4 to L5 interspace; the adult conus level is given as L1 to L2 with normal variation.
The cell count cutoff in Guillain-Barré syndrome (under 10 typical, above 50 suggesting another diagnosis) follows common diagnostic criteria; confirm the figure NABNE uses.
The mechanism of raised pressure in cryptococcal meningitis (capsular polysaccharide obstructing arachnoid granulations) is widely taught but not fully established.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Kernohan notch, Duret hemorrhage, Cushing triad, foramina of Monro, Magendie, and Luschka, or only descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: meninges-coronal (skull, dura, arachnoid, pia, sinus, bridging vein, granulation, with the three hemorrhage sites) and herniation-coronal (subfalcine, uncal, and tonsillar herniation on one coronal section).
